newsitem.title: USA: Schering-Plough says Claritin is safe.
newsitem.headline: Schering-Plough says Claritin is safe.

text.p: Two cases of liver ailments were possibly associated with the anti-histamine loratadine, sold by Schering-Plough Corp under the name Claritin, a medicaljournal reported, but Schering-Plough said the drug is safe.

"Clinicians should be aware of the risk for hepatotoxicity (liver toxicity) in patients treated with this drug," said the report by doctors at Temple University Hospital, published in the current issue of "Annals of Internal Medicine."
Schering-Plough said the reported links were inconclusive and it stood by the safety of the drug.
"There is nothing new in the cases cited in that publication to suggest that the excellent safety profile of loratadine has changed," Schering-Plough spokesman William O'Donnell said.
"Loratadine has been proven through more than a decade of studies and more than three billion patient days of worldwide use to be a safe and effective antihistamine," he said.

The report said one case involved a 42-year-old woman with a two-month history of abdominal pain and also of jaundice. She had been taking loratadine for 14 months for allergic arthritis but quit taking the drug after undergoing surgery for her condition.
The woman later received a liver transplant after experiencing progressive liver failure, and eventually recovered.

The second case involved a 33-year-old man with a one-week history of worsening jaundice and abdominal pain, who had been begun taking loratadine for allergies three weeks earlier, then quit after taking it for two weeks. He recovered.

The report said the man had been a heavy drinker and had tested positive for antibodies to hepatitis-C virus, but that result may have been a false-positive because no genetic traces of the virus were found. Also, the type of liver damage in the man was inconsistent with alcohol-related damage, it said.
Also, it was unknown whether the woman may have had another liver disease that could have made her susceptible to toxicity from loratadine, the report said.
The report noted there had been occurrences of liver ailments in early clinical trials of the drug, but no reports of such of such occurences had been published.

"These two cases show that loratadine may cause acute necroinflammatory liver disease that rarely results in the need for liver transplantation," the report said. "This complication may occur soon after therapy is initiated or as late as 14 months after."

However, O'Donnell said Schering-Plough had known about the woman's case since 1994, and sent the case for independent review by a liver expert, who concluded that the cause of her ailment could not be determined.
The federal Food and Drug Administration has been advised of the case and the review since 1994, he said.

He said Schering-Plough had been unaware of the case involving the man, but he noted the heavy drinking and signs of possible hepatitis-C infection in the patient, as well as use of other medicines by the man.
"We do intend to thoroughly examine the details of the case," O'Donnell said.
"Our overriding concern is the safety of patients, and we stand by it's (loratadine's) long record of safety and effectiveness," he said.
